title: Buddhist funerals
hookLine: chanting, merit made for the dead, the seventh- and forty-ninth-day rites

lines: A LAMA READING TO THE DEAD.
cards: Monks in saffron sit in a row beside a coffin in a Thai temple. A white cloth is laid across a thread that runs from the coffin to the monks, and they chant in Pali.

In a Japanese home, incense curls up before a photograph, and a priest's voice rises and falls through a sutra. In a Tibetan house, a lama reads aloud to someone who has just died, as if the person can still hear.
Three different rooms, and underneath, the same two things: the Dhamma spoken aloud, and something good done for the one who has gone. This week begins with Buddhist funerals.

teach.b: Start with the chant. At Theravada funerals, the monks may chant a verse that goes back to the Buddha's own passing.

In the Great Discourse on the Final Passing, as the Buddha dies, the god Sakka speaks it: impermanent, truly, are all conditioned things; they arise and they pass away; having arisen, they cease; their stilling is happiness.
A funeral opens by saying the plain truth out loud. Then, merit for the dead, a cousin of the sharing of merit you met early on.
In a short text called the Discourse Outside the Walls, the departed are described standing outside walls, at crossroads, by doorposts, returning to homes once theirs.

When relatives give food and drink to the monks and say, may this be for our relatives, the departed are said to share in the goodness and give thanks. Weeping and grief, the text says, do not help the dead. Giving does.
So families offer robes and food to the monks and dedicate the merit to the one who died. Then the counting of days.
In Tibetan tradition, the text often called the Tibetan Book of the Dead speaks of the in-between state after death lasting up to forty-nine days, and the lama's reading guides the person through it.
In China and Japan, tradition holds rites every seventh day until the forty-ninth, when the family gathers again. Across all three rooms, the funeral isn't only for grief.
It's something the living still get to do for the dead.

how: At Buddhist funerals monks or priests chant texts on impermanence, and families make offerings to the monastic community and dedicate the merit to the one who died; in East Asia and Tibet, rites are often held at intervals after the death up to the forty-ninth day.

o: chanting impermanence and giving in the name of the dead
prayers asking the Buddha to bring the dead back to life
a ceremony to judge where the dead person will go next

p: speaks the verse at the Buddha's passing
where the departed are said to wait
the end of the in-between in Tibet

s: in the Discourse Outside the Walls, weeping helps the dead
the text says grief does not help them; giving in their name does.
the funeral verse on impermanence goes back to the Buddha's passing
in the Great Discourse on the Final Passing, the god Sakka speaks it.
Buddhist funerals look the same everywhere
Thai, Japanese and Tibetan rooms differ, but chanting and merit run through them.

games.q: your relative has died. in the Discourse Outside the Walls, what helps them?
o: giving to the monks and dedicating it to them.
games.why: the text says grief doesn't reach the dead. a gift given in their name does, and they share in the goodness.

practice: This one may be tender; skip it if today isn't the day.
Bring to mind one person who has died, their face or their voice; then think of one good thing you've done or could do, and if it feels right, let it rest there: may some of this goodness reach them.
If missing someone feels too heavy to carry alone, call or text 988 in the US, or local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Buddhist funerals. Chanting the truth of impermanence, giving in the name of the dead, and marking the days that follow. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: 'impermanent, truly, are conditioned things', the opening of a verse chanted at Theravada funerals.

carryVoice: Your line: merit for the dead. Even a small kindness can be given in someone's name. Gently, until tomorrow.
